title: A Brief Treatise on Illuminating the Mind and Seeing the Nature
author: By Master Yinyuan
excerpt: We sentient beings, from beginningless vast eons, have lost our original face. Taking the false as true, calling the servant the master, we vainly give rise to greed and anger, create karma and receive retribution. Like the spring silkworm making its cocoon, we bind and entangle ourselves, with no time of liberation. The foolish, without wisdom, rest in hardship and do not seek liberation; the wise, though they know that birth and death is a great matter and the sea of suffering is boundless, desire to seek liberation.

inline.s: We sentient beings, from beginningless eons, have lost our original face. Taking the false as true, calling the servant the master, we vainly give rise to greed and anger, create karma and receive retribution. Like the spring silkworm spinning its cocoon, we bind and entangle ourselves, with no time of liberation. The foolish, without wisdom, rest in hardship and do not seek liberation; the wise, though they know birth and death is a great matter and the sea of suffering is boundless, desire liberation yet find no gate. Like the six non-Buddhist masters of old, who probed the origin of the myriad things: whether a divine self, a dark principle, or annihilation. The science and philosophy of today speak either of dualism or monism. Though each claims precisely and exhausts the mysterious, all are like the blind men feeling the elephant — none is right.

Sakyamuni Buddha, pitying sentient beings who had no way out of suffering, appeared in the world to teach them. For forty-nine years, in accord with the seasons and capacities, he spoke the great and the small, the partial and the perfect, the sudden and the gradual; with utmost sincerity and painstaking exposition he revealed two roots: the first, the root of beginningless birth and death; the second, the originally pure body of bodhi and nirvana. Thus he clarified the mystery of human life and the universe, revealed the cause of the wheel of birth and death, so that sentient beings might know their own mind and see their own nature, return to the true and constant, escape birth and death, and still the wheel of suffering.

We sentient beings originally possess the Tathagata’s wisdom and virtuous form, spiritual, bright, empty, and still, no different from the Buddha. Only because of ignorance and non-awareness, inverted and deluded grasping, and ceaseless agitation, we create karma and receive retribution; then from shared karma the mountains, rivers, and great earth are manifested, and from individual karma the twelve classes of beings (the twelve life-forms: womb-born, egg-born, moisture-born, transformation-born, and so on) are drawn forth. Thus round and round, endlessly revolving, so birth and death revolve without rest. Now, wishing to return to the original and escape birth and death, one must first awaken and break through ignorance. For if ignorance is not broken, one is lost in self and pursues objects, and when one meets a state the mind arises — then birth and death can never be ended.

Therefore all the sutras and treatises and all the Dharma gates revolve around this one center — illuminating the mind and seeing the nature — expounding and disclosing it, so that people may awaken and break through delusion, dispel ignorance, leave the false and return to the true, and find the way home. What distinguishes Buddhism from other teachings and transcends the non-Buddhist schools is that it strikes at the very root of sentient beings’ birth and death and their return to extinction. And this root lies in whether one illuminates the mind and sees the nature; hence illuminating the mind and seeing the nature is truly the essence of Buddhism and the crucial key to transcending birth and death.
[Return to extinction] To return to extinction, that is, to cultivate the Way and realize nirvana.

For this reason, though the sutras and treatises are many and their expositions and eulogies may differ, the aim is one; though the Dharma gates are broad and their means and methods may differ, the goal is the same. This is what is meant: expedient means have many gates, but the return to the source has no two paths.

But alas, down to the recent age of the Dharma’s end, scholars within the teaching have greatly gone astray. Not only do they dare not advocate and spread the great, profound, and essential purport of ‘illuminating the mind and seeing the nature’ — the very soul of this age’s teaching — but rather, as if speaking of tigers changes their complexion, they dare not even utter the phrase ‘illuminating the mind and seeing the nature’ in speech or see it in writings, and widely publicize it. Looking into it carefully, the reasons are nothing more than the following:

(1) Practitioners of the Chan school, lacking a qualified teacher, have no one to guide them in their practice, or to point things out at the right moment, to strike home with hammer and tongs and sever their clinging bonds; and at the critical juncture no one opens the right eye for them to see the original face themselves. Most take up a single formulaic ‘hua tou’ (word-topic) — ‘Who is reciting the Buddha’s name?’ — and painstakingly practice for decades with no news, no sign. Thus they regard seeing the nature as an extremely profound and difficult matter, high and beyond reach; they push it up to the realm of the sages, dare not aspire to it, and still less dare to advocate or spread it.

(2) Most Pure Land practitioners say its method is unlike all others — it advocates horizontal transcendence to birth in the West and needs no seeing the nature. Little do they know the Pure Land is a great teaching embracing the three capacities: toward the lower it stresses only horizontal transcendence, but in fact has long hidden the essential meaning of seeing the nature within the method. Consider its practice: when reciting the Buddha one must ‘unify the six sense faculties and sustain pure thought, thought after thought.’ Is this ‘unifying the six sense faculties’ not simply letting everything go? Without letting go, can one close the gates of the six faculties and gather seeing, hearing, knowing, feeling all into one Buddha-name? To recite the Buddha ceaselessly with a pure mind is to use the Buddha-thought to secretly transform deluded thought. A person cannot be without thought; if not thinking of Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha, then thinking of greed, anger, ignorance. By an expedient, one Buddha-name replaces deluded thought, so that unconsciously the deluded mind becomes the Buddha-mind. As it is said: ‘Throw the Buddha-name into the chaotic mind, and the chaotic mind cannot but become Buddha!’ Pray tell: what is the Buddha? If not seeing the nature, then what?

The school goes further, saying: ‘Entering samadhi is the foremost.’ Pray tell: what is samadhi? Samadhi is the same as samapatti [the threefold concentration]. When one recites the Buddha and realizes samadhi, the mind that recites and the Buddha that is recited fall away at once — this is the time when the sense faculties and sense-objects fall away and the subject and object are both extinguished. Reciting the Buddha to this point is the time when the bucket-bottom of the Chan school falls out, the time of illuminating the mind and seeing the nature. At this point, what is left of purity and Chan? Hence it is said that purity is Chan, and Chan is purity; Chan and the Pure Land are not two separate households.

For those of lower capacity, there is no need to speak much of deep Chan principle; just teach them to cast down body and mind and recite straightforwardly. When they recite to the point that feelings die and the mind is empty, they will naturally realize it. If those of highest capacity hear it once and awaken, still less need be said. Hence it is precisely those of lower and highest capacity who most easily attain accomplishment in the Pure Land school. For those of middle capacity seem clever without being truly clever, and seem dull without being truly dull. Not being truly clever, they cannot easily see through worldly conditions and let everything go; not being truly dull, they are unwilling to stand on solid ground and earnestly and sincerely recite the Buddha’s name. So they do not easily attain accomplishment.

Moreover, most contemporary practitioners of the Pure Land school only seek to spare themselves effort, relying solely on Amitabha Buddha’s reception and guidance to be reborn in the West. They are unwilling to exert themselves in the practice of Buddha-recitation to sweep away the deluded mind and habitual defilements and to transform themselves, but beautify it by saying: ‘We are a school of the power of others; we practice by relying on the power of others.’ When they hear ‘undivided thought,’ they shake their heads repeatedly, saying: ‘Not needed, not needed! The Pure Land only requires faith and vow; Amitabha will naturally receive us — whether one’s practice is effective or not is irrelevant.’ What need have they for ‘illuminating the mind and seeing the nature’! And how do they know that ‘undivided thought — the flower opens and one sees the Buddha and realizes non-birth’ is a synonym for illuminating the mind and seeing the nature!

(3) Practitioners of the Esoteric school, again, mostly tend toward spiritual powers and the mysterious and wonderful; some even flaunt themselves before the world to satisfy their worldly reputation and profit, and utterly disregard the practice of realizing the essence, awakening to the Way, and transcending birth and death. They have made the fine Esoteric school utterly demonic. The ‘becoming a Buddha in this life’ or ‘in this very body’ that the Esoteric school advertises — that is, illuminating the mind and seeing the nature — has long been cast beyond the clouds.

Our country’s three great schools are so weakened and disordered; other schools that exist in name only need not be spoken of, as can be imagined. Thus the whole, brilliant, radiant Buddhism has been spoiled by its unadvanced descendants into such a murky and wretched state. How do newcomers know where the essence of Buddhism lies! And how can they cultivate themselves, nourish their nature, return to heavenly truth, and transcend birth and death? To speak of this, how can one not be heartbroken and gnash the teeth!

What is more, Buddhism is a great teaching that educates people to know truth, abandon vain views, turn from evil to good, and transform humanity; it is the wholesome Dharma that awakens people from the dream of delusion, making them not cling, not be selfish, and do their utmost in benefiting all living beings; and it is the wonderful Dharma that makes sentient beings dispel delusion and realize truth, put down the heavy burden, and live lightly, joyfully, and with real benefit. Hence it is a great religion of immense practical and positive significance to society and state. For the unrest of society and the upheavals of nations are all wrought by the three root-vices of greed, anger, and ignorance. Because material desires are fierce and greed soars, people stop at nothing to commit graft, speculation, smuggling, bribery, even factionalism for private gain and plotting rebellion. And Buddhism is what takes a knife to these three poison roots.

As for the course of the world and the lot of humanity, both are retributions drawn by people’s own ignorance and deluded activity and attachment to states, creating karma. In other words, all are self-inflicted, having nothing to do with ghosts and spirits. And so long as people swiftly awaken, know their own mind and see their own nature, everyone can become a Buddha. Buddhism is a broad and great teaching that advocates perfect equality, with no distinction of class. For this reason, many hold that Buddhism is a non-religion.

Further, from the Buddhist aim, the perfect and sudden teaching says there is no birth and death to escape, no nirvana to realize, no Buddha and no sentient beings, and every dharma is empty. To stir a thought is to depart from one’s own school; ‘to raise the mind is to be wrong; to move a thought is to depart.’ It takes no-aim as its aim, which is the true aim, because to have an aim is to fall into a one-sided view. Hence many call it a non-religion. But they forget that though it takes no-aim as its aim, it is not without a master; there is still an ‘aim of having no aim,’ so it is also not a non-religion. Because it has no aim, one should not call it a religion; because it takes no-aim as its aim, one should not call it not a religion. Not empty and not existent, not existent and not empty — this is the essential meaning of its Middle Way, which establishes no two extremes; to grasp it, one must illuminate the mind and see the nature! Hence seeing the nature is of utmost importance for students of the Buddha.

Since illuminating the mind and seeing the nature is so important to students of the Buddha, what exactly does its content consist of? How can one attain it? What is the state when one realizes it? And what is its function after realization? These many questions are what students of the Buddha should understand and urgently investigate. For the sake of clarity and ease, and to facilitate the reader’s attainment, I will briefly set them out below, each in turn.

blocks.text: I. The Meaning of Illuminating the Mind and Seeing the Nature

inline.s: Illuminating the mind and seeing the nature’, put simply and comprehensively, means: by investigating the form and function of the human ‘mind,’ to see through to, realize, and spiritually comprehend the root of life — the wonderful substance and truth of ‘the nature’ — so as to awaken from the dream of delusion, transcend birth and death, and realize great nirvana. Analyzed in detail, its meaning is extremely profound and broad, for it is the very essence of this age’s teaching; one may say that the three baskets and the twelve divisions are all its commentary. Here we can only select the essential and speak of it briefly.

Before discussing the content of illuminating the mind and seeing the nature and how to do it, let us first sketch the outline of mind and nature, so that it is easier to begin analyzing and discussing the meaning of illuminating the mind and seeing the nature.

So what is mind? And what is nature? The so-called mind is not the lump of flesh in the chest, but the thoughts that arise when we meet a state; the scriptures call it the shadow cast by the six sense-objects upon conditions — the faded shadows of form, sound, smell, taste, touch, and dharmas — abbreviated as: gathered-up and arising is mind. Originally we have no mind, but because these objects are present we receive their images from each condition, distinguish their sameness and difference, establish names, give rise to love and anger, grasping and rejecting, and only then does the variety of thoughts arise. This mind arises from gathering together with the environment, hence it is called gathered-up-and-arising mind — what modern theory calls ‘thought is the reflection of the objective environment.’ The Faxiang school’s Treatise on the Establishment of Consciousness-Only explains this clearly: eight great mind-kings and fifty-one mental factors. To save space I will not detail it here; let the reader study that treatise.

Since mind is thus, what is nature? Nature is the root that gives rise to mind, the origin of mind. Modern theory holds that it is the energy that gives rise to mind. Without it, one cannot give rise to mind when meeting a state. That we can give rise to mind upon meeting a state is entirely its function. It is without form and without characteristics, so the eye cannot see it; yet it can give rise to all kinds of functions, so it truly exists. The ancients compared it to the glue within paint and the salt in water — though not visible to the eye, it truly functions and works. In the scriptures it has many different names, such as the one-real dharma-realm, thusness, the tathagatagarbha, Buddha-nature, the true mind, the great perfect sublime wisdom, and so on. (Editor’s note: if the reader finds it difficult here, it is suggested to read first the
Mind, Self-Nature, and Tathagatagarbha
article, and then read this piece; you will then get twice the result with half the effort.)

Only because sentient beings are deluded and unaware, not knowing this wonderful substance, from beginningless time they have combined only with arising and ceasing, turning it into a deluded mind. Hence mind and nature are originally one thing, like water and its waves, not two matters. That the world now leaps forward depends on automation, and automation on electrical energy; without energy there is no motive power; without motive power everything is static and dead. Likewise that we can think, work, create, and invent depends on the motive power within the body, and this power is the nature’s function. So though nature cannot be seen by the eye, it truly functions in everything, just as electricity, though invisible, works in all lighting and motion. The scriptures call nature substance and mind function, nature principle and mind phenomenon. But the Chan school often uses the two interchangeably; we need only grasp their depths and distinction, and we will not be confused.

Having understood the form and definition of mind and nature, one must go further to investigate how ‘nature’ — the root of life — gives rise to mind upon meeting a state; and why state arises, so that birth and death wind on without end. One must also understand what the meaning of illuminating the mind and seeing the nature includes; and how one can illuminate it and see it, and escape birth and death. Now let us divide this into five sections and discuss it in detail.
Illuminating the mind and seeing the nature means to illuminate that the mind is false and unattainable, and, stilling the frantic mind, to see the true nature.

We who wish to transcend birth and death must first know the origin of birth and death. If one wishes to cut off a stream, one must first know where its source lies, and then one can stop up its source and cut off its stream, roaming freely beyond birth and death. So how does the multitude of sentient beings, rising and sinking within the six realms in endless revolution, arise in the first place?

Sakyamuni Buddha told us in two phrases: ‘The three realms are mind-only; the myriad dharmas are consciousness-only.’ This means all sentient beings originally possess the tathagatagarbha nature, a universal substance — unborn and undying, undefiled and unpurified, not coming and not going, formless and spiritual; it does not belong to delusion or enlightenment. Only because beings are unaware and do not know the wonderful substance is originally luminous do they give rise to a single thought of recognizing luminosity, turning the luminous wisdom-radiance into the false-luminance of misguided cognition. They divide what was originally one awakened-luminance into the opposition of awakening and luminance — awakening has luminance outside it, luminance has awakening outside it — thus establishing subject and object. This is what the Surangama Sutra means by ‘the nature’s awakening must be luminous; this is falsely taken as the luminous awakening.’

Because of this ignorance (the luminous awakening we call ignorance), the original perfect luminance is lost, and the formless true suchness is turned into the alaya consciousness (like a man drunk with wine). Thus spiritual bright emptiness becomes dull emptiness; within it ignorance stirs and condenses into the four great false forms (earth, water, fire, wind, inherent in the tathagatagarbha nature, manifesting through deluded stirring; the world is coagulated from these four greats). This is what the Surangama Sutra means by ‘delusion and error create empty space; relying on emptiness, the world is established.’ Because of these false forms, the present radiant wisdom is turned into false perception, which takes them as the seen states. False perception, enduring, grasps a portion of the four greats as ‘self,’ entrusting itself to them as its own body — ignorance envelops the eighth consciousness and submerges it into the body-root. The four greats are without consciousness, but through false perception’s grasping become conscious. The true mind is immeasurable, but is sealed by ignorance and submerges into the four greats as its mind. This is ‘form mixed with delusion; the thought-image is taken as body,’ the sentient being of the five aggregates; as the Surangama Sutra says: ‘thought settling becomes lands and states; perception and cognition are sentient beings.’

From this it can be seen that the false arising of body, mind, and world is truly the fault of the single thought of recognizing luminosity (that is, ignorance). Since sentient beings have lost their true nature and take things as self, they pursue objects and states, cling to them without abandoning, create karma and receive retribution, revolving endlessly! The sutra says: ‘When the mind arises, all dharmas arise; when dharmas arise, all minds arise.’ Seeds produce manifestations, and manifestations in turn perfum the seeds; from cause comes fruit, and fruit in turn draws cause; cause and fruit, fruit and cause, round and round, endlessly. Hence sentient beings, within what is without birth and death, vainly undergo the suffering of the wheel of birth and death, and never find rest!

Therefore it is said that the human mind is false and unreal. It is only the shadow cast by the six sense-objects upon conditions, and the six sense-objects are themselves illusorily manifested by the deluded knotting of ignorance, and are originally unattainable. The scriptures speak of not self-arising, not other-arising, not both-arising, not causeless arising. And the deluded mind that arises from it is even more delusion within delusion. The modern philosophers also say that ‘mind’ is the reflection of objective matter, but they only say that mind is produced by matter, without pointing out what produces matter; this is not as complete as the scriptures. The Buddha said: ‘Mind is not mind by itself; because of things, mind exists; things are not things by themselves; because of mind, things exist.’ This sets clearly and completely the principle of the illusory arising of mind and things as each other’s cause and effect.

Since mind and things are both illusory and unattainable, once we awaken from the dream and realize that body, mind, and world are originally empty, this is illuminating the mind. In this original emptiness, one is not like wood or stone, without knowledge or feeling, but empty, luminous, and knowingly aware; though empty, luminous, and aware, yet still and unmoving, with no thought arising — what is this? This wondrous yet plain scene — if it is not our unborn, undying, eternally abiding true-suchness substance, then what is it! When this substance suddenly reveals itself, to seize it at once is called personally realizing the original face, and is also called seeing the nature.

The so-called seeing the nature is not seeing anything with the eyes, but the intimate and profound realization and spiritual comprehension of the Dharma-eye of the mind-ground. The sutra says: ‘At the time of seeing, the seeing is not seeing.’ Hence illuminating the mind and seeing the nature is to thoroughly see the true nature at the point where false knowledge and false views are broken, when the frantic mind ceases and body and mind dissolve.

The Second Patriarch, the Great Master Shenguang, went to see the First Patriarch Bodhidharma and said: ‘My mind is not at peace; pray pacify my mind.’ The Patriarch said: ‘Bring your mind to me, and I will pacify it.’ After a while the master said: ‘I have searched for the mind, and it is unattainable.’ The Patriarch, following with the current, said: ‘I have pacified your mind!’ And the master awakened greatly. This is to see through, at the point where the mind is unattainable (the former thought ceased, the latter not yet arisen), this lucid, knowing nature that does not fall into annihilation (the thought was cut off, but not like wood or stone). The beauty of this gong’an is that mind is a gathering of the false with no real place of coming; once pressed, it dissolves. But though thought ceases and is empty, the capacity (nature) is not extinguished; one who at that moment turns the light back and grasps it sees the nature. The indestructibility of energy, scientists all admit; and the greatest energy is the nature’s capacity. For nature is formless, greatest and hardest — great without outside, small without inside; it can crush all things, and nothing can crush it, so it cannot be measured. What takes rebirth in the six realms is it; what transcends birth and death is also it.

blocks.text: (II) The Wondrous Function of Illuminating the Mind

inline.s: Illuminating the mind and seeing the nature means to understand that the wondrous functions of the mind all arise from the nature-substance; from function one sees substance, from the stream one reaches the source.

A master of old said: The substance has no form; without function it is not manifested; the nature has no appearance; without mind it is not known! To put forth function is to manifest substance; to illuminate the mind is to see the nature. Hence to see the nature one must start from illuminating the mind; apart from the mind there is no nature to see. For the nature-substance has no image and cannot be seen, while the mind is function, and function without form is not manifested. From the formed mind-function one can see the formless nature-substance. Our thoughts, work, inventions, and today’s civilization are all functions of the mind. To see the nature one must see it from these functions; apart from function there is no nature to see. Like principle and phenomena: without principle nothing is accomplished, without phenomena principle is not manifested. Principle is phenomena, phenomena is principle; they are not separate. Hence to see principle one must see it from phenomena.

King Yijian asked the Venerable Bharata: ‘What is the Buddha?’ He said: ‘Seeing the nature is the Buddha!’ The king said: ‘Do you see the nature?’ He said: ‘I see the Buddha-nature.’ ‘Where is the nature?’ ‘The nature is in function!’ ‘What function? I do not see it.’ ‘The function is bright and manifest; you yourself do not see it!’ ‘Is it within me?’ ‘If the king functions, all is right; if not, the substance is hard to see.’ ‘When in use, in how many places does it appear?’ ‘There are eight.’ ‘Tell me the eight.’ ‘In the womb it is the body; in the world a person; in the eye seeing; in the ear hearing; in the nose distinguishing smell; in the tongue speaking; in the hand grasping; in the foot running. Everywhere manifest it covers the dharma-realm; gathered, it is in a single dust-mote. The one who knows knows it is the Buddha-nature; the one who does not calls it the soul!’ The king, hearing this, awakened.

Again, take the Diamond Sutra: why did the World-Honored One, before speaking the Dharma, first insert a passage about putting on his robe, holding his bowl, entering the city, and begging for food, up to his sitting upon the seat? Because he wished to awaken the opportunity of the formless prajna of the assembly, and had to borrow the formed forms of the six perfections. For without substance, function cannot be accomplished; the forms and functions all about are everywhere manifesting in reverse the formless substance of prajna. But we do not recognize it; hence the Buddha specially borrows formed actions to secretly display the formless wonderful substance, to cause us to realize the prajna paramita.

Nature is indeed not without existence, but it cannot be heard with the ear, cannot be seen with the eye, cannot be known with knowledge, cannot be cognized with cognition; but it can be illumined with wisdom, contemplated with wonderful insight, realized, and spiritually comprehended. Hence it is said: ‘Thus comprehend; comprehend thus’ and nothing more. The secret action of the six perfections is the Buddha’s wordless teaching. Such prajna radiating its light, alone Subhuti understood it at once, and responding to the occasion arose and came forth to ask, thereby accomplishing the wonderful Diamond Prajna Sutra.

blocks.text: (III) The Illumined Mind Is Originally Nonexistent

inline.s: Illuminating the mind and seeing the nature means to illuminate that the mind is originally nonexistent, and to see the nature that is originally existent.

As said above, mind and nature are like function and principle-substance. Function, though it has form and can be seen by the eye, seems to exist but is truly nonexistent, because of dependent-origination and the emptiness of nature; the principle-substance, though without form to be seen, seems nonexistent but truly exists, because of the emptiness of nature and dependent-origination. The two are mutually supportive: apart from substance there is no form, apart from form there is no substance. Hence it is said: not empty and not existent, also empty and also existent, empty and existent. We must not only not cling to any of the phenomenal forms, biased to one side, but must also see through the illusorily arisen phenomena to perceive the true and real nature-substance.

The Surangama Sutra says: ‘The nature of form is true emptiness; the nature of emptiness is true form.’ The nature-substance is true emptiness, without form and image; it is the formless true emptiness that is the nature-substance. All formed colors are false forms. False forms have no substance, like flowers in the sky and the moon in water, unattainable — mere delusion. Hence the Heart Sutra says all things are without: without the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, mind and form, sound, smell, taste, touch, and dharmas of the worldly dharmas; also without the suffering, origin, cessation, and path and the twelve links of dependent origination of the hearers and pratyekabuddhas; moreover without the wisdom and gain of the bodhisattvas; and at the point where all is unattainable, one attains anuttara-samyak-sambodhi. This reveals that we, at the point where the mind that should be illumined is nonexistent, thoroughly see the originally present nature-substance.

In the Chan school this is the school of extinction and non-commitment. Layman Pang asked Mazu: ‘The one who is not the companion of the myriad things — what kind of person is he?’ Mazu said: ‘Wait until you drink up the Western River in one gulp, and then I will tell you!’ When thoughts are extinguished and emptiness and existence both dissolve, the true empty wonderful substance naturally manifests. Again, the master Chuquan visited the Dharma-Master of Mount Chishan. One day the master asked: ‘The Lotus Sutra reveals, shows, awakens, and leads one to enter the Buddha’s knowledge and vision; every past patriarch has had his own exposition. But these are each patriarch’s own, not yours. Now say it from your own breast: how to reveal, show, awaken, and lead one to enter that knowledge and vision?’ He was silent. The old master sighed: ‘Meditating thus is only wasting time — what benefit?’ He made him meditate kneeling. After three incense sticks, hearing the rector strike the wood to end the sitting, he suddenly awoke! ‘How do you reveal the Buddha’s knowledge?’ ‘Revealing the originally present (the originally present self-nature principle-substance).’ ‘How do you show?’ ‘Showing the originally nonexistent (all the mind’s functions and forms are unattainable; from the unattainable function one shows the true original substance).’ ‘How do you awaken?’ ‘Awakening to the nonexistence of existence and nonexistence (erasing the traces of delusion and awakening).’ ‘How do you enter?’ ‘Entering without obstruction (attaining great freedom; in speech, silence, movement, stillness, free and unobstructed).’

blocks.text: (IV) Illuminating That Mind Is Nature and Nature Is Mind

inline.s: Illuminating the mind and seeing the nature means to awaken to the truth that mind is nature and nature is mind.

Zen Master Zhenjue said: Though mind and nature seem to have the distinction of substance and function, principle and phenomenon, yet examining their reality, they are neither one nor different. Speaking from phenomena, the wonderful function follows conditions and responds, manifesting all kinds, and seems to have form and image, while the wonderful substance is unmoving, transcending all opposition, and apart from all characteristics — hence not one. But function springs from substance, and function does not leave substance; substance can put forth function, and substance does not leave function; speaking from their not being mutually opposed, they are not different. The sutra says: ‘All phenomenal forms are manifestations of the nature.’ Though phenomena differ, classed and categorized, each being different, yet their nature is one. Hence it is said: ‘Nothing does not flow from this dharma-realm; nothing does not return to this dharma-realm.’

A bright mirror cannot but reflect images; without images it would not be a bright mirror. The images all come from the bright mirror; without the mirror, images cannot be reflected. Mind and nature are likewise: nature is the true-empty wonderful substance, mind is the formed function. Hence where there is the nature-substance, there must be form-function; without form, neither can substance be manifested. Thus form is nature, and nature is form; apart from form there is no nature, apart from nature there is no form. It is not like dull emptiness, which is stubborn and unspiritual, dead and still and unknowing, falling into annihilation.

Sentient beings lose their head and take the shadow, cling to form and create karma, and so draw the defiled land with the five turbidities. The Buddhas see the nature and abandon form, pure and undefiled, and so experience the adorned Pure Land. Though the true and false, the pure and defiled differ, the nature-substance that manifests form is one. We need only convert the error of taking the shadow and rejecting the mirror into taking the mirror and rejecting the shadow, and the defiled land is at once the Pure Land, without waiting until after death to attain rebirth. The sutra says: ‘As the mind is pure, the Buddha-land is pure; to purify the land, first purify the mind’ — and rightly so.

‘True empty wonderful existence’ distinguishes from dull emptiness; it is putting forth function from the substance. Because of true emptiness, it can accord with conditions; because of wonderful existence, it can function. ‘Wonderful existence true emptiness’ distinguishes from real existence; it is gathering function back into the substance. Because it accords with conditions and functions, manifesting various illusory forms, the Amitabha Sutra speaks of the Buddha-land’s adornment; because the nature-substance is pure and undefiled, not touching a single dharma, the Diamond Sutra speaks of not a single thing being established. Not a single thing being established is precisely the adornment of the Buddha-land; the adornment of the Buddha-land is precisely not a single thing being established. Hence the Diamond is the Amitabha, and the Amitabha is the Diamond — they are not two kinds.

Mind, nature, form, and substance — they seem different but are in truth one, like water and its waves: water takes wetness as substance, and waves take movement as form. The water’s nature and the wave’s form seem not one, but the wave is the water and the water is the wave; the wet nature is not different. Hence one who truly sees the nature can not only see the Way with the Dharma-eye of the mind-ground, but the physical eye can also see through to the true nature. Because nature is form and form is nature. A master of old said: ‘In the midst of the myriad forms, alone the body is revealed!’ And again: ‘The mountains, rivers, and the great earth all reveal the body of the Dharma King!’ — meaning that all the existent things of this world are manifestations of my nature-substance.

The Diamond Sutra says: ‘If one sees all forms as non-forms, one sees the Tathagata!’ If we can truly investigate this principle, and in daily life see the nature right within form, not treating any of the conditions and states as conditions and states, then at once we transcend all existence and roam beyond the three realms! Being born, preaching, hard rocks nodding — sentient and insentient alike perfectly perfect the wisdom of all modes. What the eye reaches and what the ear hears, all are the Buddha. In the Chan school this is called directly pointing to the mind-nature. For example, Damei asked Mazu: ‘What is the Buddha?’ Mazu said: ‘Mind is Buddha!’ And Damei awakened greatly at those words. Again, Lingxun asked Master Guizong: ‘What is the Buddha?’ Guizong said: ‘I now tell you, but I fear you will not believe!’ Lingxun said: ‘The Master’s sincere word — how would I dare not believe!’ Guizong said: ‘You yourself are it!’ And Lingxun awakened. See how decisive! How direct! How joyful!

blocks.text: (V) Illuminating That the Mind-Nature Abides Nowhere

inline.s: Illuminating the mind and seeing the nature means to illuminate that the mind-nature abides nowhere, not a single thing is established, and one returns to having nothing attained.

The mind-nature is originally empty and spiritual, abiding nowhere, and only so becomes wonderful function; the moment it abides somewhere it becomes a nest and rut. It originally has not a single thing; speaking of empty or existent, delusion or awakening, true or false, are all oppositions and idle talk. Whatever is spoken, none has real meaning. If one thoroughly awakens to the source of mind and sees the true nature, since delusion does not exist, where could awakening stand? Not establishing is also not not-establishing; not a single dharma is attainable. Hence the emptiness of self is not true emptiness; one must have the emptiness of dharmas, and furthermore the emptiness of emptiness, before truly arriving home. As the ancients said: having nothing accomplished, nothing attained, nothing cultivated, nothing realized — only this is true accomplishment, attainment, and realization. If one thinks one has a dharma to attain and a Way to accomplish, one has fallen into the dharma-clinging of the sage-stage. At the least one cannot end birth and death; even ending the segmental birth and death, one can never end the transformation birth and death, because dharma-clinging is its obstacle. At the greatest one goes mad and becomes a demon, and the consequences are unthinkable!

The saying about no cultivation, no attainment, no realization is the transcendent speech of one who has awakened and arrived home, and also the ground-teaching of one who first understands the Tathagata’s secret cause. Because sentient beings are originally the Buddha, not made so by cultivation. Only through non-awareness, losing self and pursuing objects, chasing external states, do they sink to being sentient beings. Now if one sharply awakens, like a dark room of a thousand years lit by a single lamp, one returns to the original nature — what cultivation or realization can be spoken of? Hence one does not need toil and painstaking realization. But if one’s habitual defilements are deep and clinging grave, though one understands this principle, the mind arises when meeting a state, and then there is indeed the unsparing, fine, continuous work of sweeping! Again, if one only understands the principle but has not personally seen the self-nature, and merely has the cause for future buddhahood, one must the more diligently cultivate to realize it. Do not on any account speak big, deceive yourself and others, and deny cultivation and realization only to meet a reckless disaster.

Thoroughly awakening to the mind-nature, not a single dharma is established, no Buddha and no sentient beings; all day as if foolish and stupid, moving freely with conditions — all is Buddha-work. The so-called smiling and laughing, anger and abuse, coughing and waving the arm — all are the ocean-seal radiating light; putting on clothes and eating, carrying water and carrying firewood — none are not spiritual powers and wondrous functions! In all this there is nothing grasped and nothing rejected, nothing relied upon and nothing set upon, hence it is called returning to having nothing attained.
